    <title>Taiwan's troops are training to fight China in ordinary neighborhoods as people go about their days</title>
    <updated>2026-08-24T04:59:13Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/taiwan-troops-train-fight-china-ordinary-neighborhood-public-han-kuang-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a87b9ee8a99fa493d60e9f9?format=jpeg" height="2000" width="3000" alt="A Taiwanese military police soldier carries a Kestrel anti-armor weapon as a civilian looks on."><figcaption>Taiwan&#39;s Han Kuang exercises are carried out right in the middle of neighborhoods and city streets.<p class="copyright">Ann Wang/REUTERS</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Taiwan held a slew of military exercises this month to simulate a Chinese invasion.</li><li>For 10 days and 9 nights, its troops skirmished and drilled in public view on city streets and alleys.</li><li>The island hopes to help people become familiar with the military and think about war scenarios.</li></ul><p>TAIPEI — Phone in hand, the middle-aged woman gestured to the Taipei intersection, where an infantry platoon unloaded sandbags on the pedestrian crossings.</p><p>"My Uber is waiting for me just there," she said in Mandarin, pointing behind them. The bespectacled military policeman blocking her path with a T112 assault rifle apologized: She'd have to find another way around.</p><p>Soon after, Clouded Leopard infantry fighting vehicles emerged between the shophouses, opening fire with blanks into a killbox the Taiwanese formed with barricades. Military police covered the roads with smoke grenades, several leapfrogging through the streets under covering fire to regroup with the main force.</p><p>The drill, a simulation of a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/china-victory-taiwan-single-river-tamsui-taipei-trianing-defend-2026-8">bridge defense against Chinese forces</a>, was held after midnight to minimize disruption to the capital's Wanhua cultural district. But with much of <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/taiwan-cm-11-brave-tiger-frankenstein-tank-tamsui-guard-china-2026-8">Taiwan's Han Kuang exercise </a>conducted in the bustle of its cities and neighborhoods, it's clear the military wants to train its troops on the very streets they're assigned to defend — while still letting the rest of the island go about its business.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8badf08a99fa493d60f4a0?format=jpeg" height="2032" width="3609" alt="A woman in a mask speaks to a Taiwanese soldier."><figcaption>The military police started turning people around as the drill was due to start, though others later wandered onto the scene.<p class="copyright">Matthew Loh for Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure><p>The practice adds an element of realism to the live drills, giving way to odd scenes where infantry and armored brigades engaged in mock skirmishes or counter-sabotage operations right next to people walking their dogs, going out for a party, or simply living at home.</p><p>Troops in urban areas used blanks instead of live ammunition, which was fired only on <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/how-china-could-quickly-seize-key-islands-from-taiwan-2024-8">Taiwan's outlying islands.</a></p><p>In a residential area south of the Songshan airport, diners sidled out from a barbecue restaurant to gawk at troops firing blanks from alleys and rooftops. Halfway through the drill, a police cruiser showed up, apparently investigating a noise complaint.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8bb8a74569a4ec219f954a?format=jpeg" height="1222" width="2311" alt="Three Taiwanese men watch soldiers open fire from an alley near Songshan Airport."><figcaption>Taiwanese troops open fire behind a gate as diners watch on.<p class="copyright">Matthew Loh for Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure><p>And in the southern city of Kaohsiung, a delivery worker on a scooter sped past a guard to drop off the mail at an auto shop, as reservists lined the main road with busted cars, barbed wire, and fortifications.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8baaff1d1a1d028ba12268?format=jpeg" height="2244" width="2992" alt="A deliveryman lifts up a package from his scooter basket."><figcaption>A delivery worker drops off the mail at this auto shop as reservists set up a blockade on the roads.<p class="copyright">Matthew Loh for Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure><p>Several dozen yards away, a softball team practiced in the late morning heat.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8baae74569a4ec219f953d?format=jpeg" height="2244" width="2992" alt="A Taiwanese reservist infantryman aims with his assault rifle near a sofa as makeshift cover."><figcaption>Reservists watched the approach on a road in Kaohsiung as a softball team practiced nearby.<p class="copyright">Matthew Loh for Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure><p>Past Han Kuang exercises often featured simulated <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/chinese-invasion-taiwan-seizing-ports-2024-12">force-on-force battles</a>, meant to show the public — and China — that Taiwan has the resolve and weapons to defend itself from an invasion. But Taipei said last year that it's reforming the Han Kuang to instead focus on unscripted exercises, hoping they would serve as better stress tests for its military and society.</p><p>"This year's Han Kuang exercise gradually shifted away from 'staged performances' designed for senior officials and the public, moving toward genuine operational verification," said Lin Ping-yu, a former Taiwanese special forces paratrooper who is now a city councilor for New Taipei City.</p><p>The result this year was dozens of logistics and combat drills peppered across the island of 23 million people.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8babd21d1a1d028ba12269?format=jpeg" height="2252" width="4000" alt="Military police forces haul a crate of ammunition on a trolley up a ramp into the exhibition center."><figcaption>Taiwanese military police hauled ammunition into the Nangang Exhibition Center visitor center on a stormy night.<p class="copyright">Matthew Loh for Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure><p>As Typhoon Dolphin brushed past Taipei, driving rainstorms into the capital on the fourth day of the exercises, military police special forces with machine guns and antitank launchers watched the late-night streets from park treelines near the Nangang Exhibition Center, Taiwan's largest trade-show complex.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8bacec1d1a1d028ba1226a?format=jpeg" height="3334" width="5000" alt="Taiwanese military police in digital camouflage sprint into Ximen Station."><figcaption>Taiwanese troops sprint into the metro station for Ximen, the popular tourist district that serves street food and snacks.<p class="copyright">Daniel Ceng/Anadolu via Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><p>The scenario assumed their command in central Taipei had suffered heavy casualties, and the survivors were retreating across the city by subway to Nangang, where the visitor center was being set up as a makeshift headquarters.</p><h2 id="309a5abd-70ab-4892-92e1-dc6560495b74" data-toc-id="309a5abd-70ab-4892-92e1-dc6560495b74">Roping in civilians</h2><p>Civilian infrastructure like this featured regularly in the drills, with reservists gathering in schools, privately owned factories converted into backup arms-production facilities, and a culture park used as a vehicle-field repair station.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8bae9b8a99fa493d60f4a1?format=jpeg" height="3695" width="5542" alt="A Patriot battery is stationed in the middle of a park in Taipei."><figcaption>Taiwan sets up Patriot surface-to-air missile batteries in some of its parks in Taipei for the Han Kuang.<p class="copyright">Daniel Ceng/Anadolu via Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><p>"If you look at the exercises as a whole, Taiwan is actually training for almost every major contingency it could face," said Tristan Tang, a Taipei-based nonresident fellow at the US think tank National Bureau of Asian Research.</p><p>Folding civilians into the war effort can get messy. On August 9, for example, a civilian truck ferrying <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/poland-boost-howitzer-155mm-shell-production-fivefold-ukraine-russia-war-2025-6">155mm howitzer shells</a> spilled its contents along a highway in Miaoli while navigating a bend.</p><p>The rounds were inert, and the military said the fastening straps on the eight-inch shells had come loose, calling it evidence that the transport operation had room for improvement.</p><p>The Han Kuang also conducted limited, citywide drills to train the public for war. For the first time, city governments throttled mobile internet for 30-minute periods during the exercise, hoping to get people thinking about how an <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/chinas-war-games-taiwan-show-air-superiority-long-range-strikes-2025-12">attack would affect communications</a>.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8baf5d1d1a1d028ba1226e?format=jpeg" height="2252" width="4000" alt="Taiwanese people wait in a subway station for the air raid drill to expire."><figcaption>In central Taipei, hundreds waited in subway stations, some of which also host underground malls. Most retail businesses closed for half an hour.<p class="copyright">Matthew Loh for Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure><p>On a Thursday afternoon, <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/taiwan-apologize-air-raid-alert-missile-satellite-china-launch-2024-1">air-raid alerts</a> buzzed on mobile phones in Taipei, ordering people to head indoors for shelter. The streets emptied, turning the capital into a ghost city for 30 minutes as people abandoned buses, cars, and motorbikes on the roads.</p><p>Lin said Taiwan previously conducted its civil and military exercises separately, and combining them was one of the most significant changes the island made this year.</p><p>"This shift helps the public grow more accustomed to the presence of military units in their daily lives," he said.</p><p>The New Taipei City Councilor, an advocate for arms innovation and <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/taiwan-needs-both-sophisticated-asymmetric-weapons-for-china-2025-12">bolstering Taiwanese defense,</a> raised concerns that years of relaxed relations with China had caused its military to "forget how to operate as a truly effective fighting force."</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8bb12a8a99fa493d60f4a2?format=jpeg" height="3701" width="5739" alt="The streets near Taipei's presidential office are completely empty for the air-raid drill."><figcaption>Millions of people went indoors for 30 minutes in Taipei.<p class="copyright">I-Hwa Cheng / AFP via Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><p>Cross-strait tensions have worsened, especially with the rise of the Democratic Progressive Party, the party of the current president, which rejects Beijing's territorial claim. China, meanwhile, has been growing <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/chinas-navy-upping-realistic-combat-training-around-taiwan-2025-3">increasingly hostile toward Taiwan,</a> with the country's leader, Xi Jinping, refusing to rule out taking the island by force.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a7a876a8fcc2e955f7df4ec?format=jpeg" height="2252" width="4000" alt="Taiwanese troops take position in a construction yard."><figcaption>This Abrams tank platoon stationed itself next to a Chinese temple, famed for a statue of Guan Yu built to look like a Lego figurine.<p class="copyright">Matthew Loh for Business Insider</p></figcaption></figure><p>With changes to drills such as the Han Kuang, Taiwan's military is in a "critical transition" phase in its warfighting capabilities, Lin said.</p><p>"We are now at a pivotal moment to reclaim these core military capabilities, and conducting more rigorous exercises will help the military rebuild its operational edge," Lin said.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/taiwan-troops-train-fight-china-ordinary-neighborhood-public-han-kuang-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-08-24T04:59:13Z</published>
    <summary type="text">For 10 days and 9 nights, Taiwanese troops skirmished and drilled in city streets and alleys, right next to diners and joggers.</summary>

    <title>‘The Odyssey’ actor John Leguizamo says his wife helps keep his ego in check</title>
    <updated>2026-08-24T04:31:50Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/odyssey-john-leguizamo-wife-keeps-him-grounded-hollywood-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8bac7d8a99fa493d60f49c?format=jpeg" height="3736" width="4981" alt="John Leguizamo."><figcaption>John Leguizamo said his wife makes sure he stays grounded.<p class="copyright">Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>"The Odyssey" actor John Leguizamo said his wife is his "moral compass."</li><li>She gives him the freedom he needs to pursue his creative work, but makes sure fame doesn't get to his head, he said.</li><li>"She'll call me out, set me straight, put me in my place," Leguizamo said.</li></ul><p><a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/john-leguizamo-movie-tv-roles-encanto-ice-age-carlitos-way-2024-5">John Leguizamo</a> said his wife makes sure the glitz of his Hollywood career doesn't go to his head.</p><p>Speaking on the "<a target="_blank" class="" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hq-bEVt_ZMo">Wild Card with Rachel Martin</a>" podcast, Leguizamo reflected on more than two decades of marriage and the role his wife plays in supporting both his personal and creative life.</p><p>"My wife is my moral compass," Leguizamo said. </p><p>Leguizamo met his wife, Justine Maurer, while working on the crime drama "Carlito's Way," in which he played an up-and-coming gangster, and she worked in the costume department.</p><p>"We dated, and then we got married. We had kids, but she's always been sort of the north star, keeping our house together, keeping me together," he said.</p><p>"<a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/odyssey-christopher-nolan-leadership-teamwork-hard-work-ethic-lessons-2026-7">The Odyssey</a>" actor said his wife understands that he needs certain freedoms and routines to create and write, and gives him the space to be the artist he wants to be.</p><p>However, her support also comes with plenty of honesty.</p><p>"She'll call me out, set me straight, put me in my place. She'll do all of that, which is great. Humbling," Leguizamo said.</p><p>He said that even after attending a premiere with Matt Damon or going to a major sporting event, Maurer makes sure he doesn't get too caught up in the glamour.</p><p>"Go take out the garbage. You're a big deal, yeah, yeah, yeah. Go clean the cat litter," Leguizamo said.</p><p>This isn't the first time Leguizamo has spoken about his relationship with his wife.</p><p>In a 2011 <a target="_blank" class="" href="https://www.aarp.org/entertainment/television/john-leguizamo-klown">interview with AARP</a>, he said his wife brought out the best in him.</p><p>"Being an actor, especially at first, tends to make you incredibly narcissistic. My wife… was my savior. I've achieved my best artistic levels, and it's all because of her," Leguizamo said.</p><p>In 2024, he <a target="_blank" class="" href="https://people.com/john-leguizamo-on-30-year-love-story-with-wife-justine-maurer-exclusive-8575623">told People</a> that Maurer had given him a sense of stability amid the demands of his Hollywood career.</p><p>"I wanted peace. I wanted to have an oasis. And Justine gave me all of that," he said.</p><p>Other celebrities have also spoken about how their spouses have <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/celebrity-couples-supportive-husbands-career-move-tayvis-tomdaya-2026-8">supported their careers</a>.</p><p>In August 2025, <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/michelle-yeoh-husband-jean-todt-support-career-relationship-strong-marriage-2025-8">Michelle Yeoh</a> said her husband, Jean Todt, has always given her the freedom to pursue her career.</p><p>"I am so blessed because he's so supportive of what I do. I love my work. This is my passion. He never turns around and says, 'You spend a lot of time away from me,' which I have sometimes, but he's very understanding," she said.</p><p>In November, <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/ina-garten-long-marriage-relationship-rule-respect-decision-making-2025-11">Ina Garten</a> said her decadeslong marriage to her husband, Jeffrey, works because they make room for both of their priorities.</p><p>"And this is what Jeffrey taught me: Let's figure out how we can both do what we want to do. It's not about whether we get to do what you want to do or I want to do," Garten said.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/odyssey-john-leguizamo-wife-keeps-him-grounded-hollywood-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-08-24T04:31:50Z</published>

    <title>I left Canada for Bangkok and now work while the city sleeps. My quality of life has never been better.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-24T02:03:02Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-to-bangkok-works-american-business-hours-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a7d7b76bd87410e364d1ec7?format=jpeg" height="1977" width="2636" alt="A man posing for a photo infront of a window."><figcaption>Francis Cloutier is a digital nomad based in Bangkok, where he works Eastern Time from halfway around the world.<p class="copyright">Provided by Francis Cloutier.</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>In 2019, Francis Cloutier left Canada to pursue a life of remote work and travel.</li><li>Most of his travels took him through South America until a friend invited him to visit Bangkok.</li><li>He now lives in Thailand with his wife and keeps Eastern Time hours, working through the night.</li></ul><p><em>This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Francis Coultier, 39, who is originally from Canada but now lives in Bangkok. It's been edited for length and clarity.</em></p><p>The first time I learned about about digital nomadism, I was around 29 and <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-new-york-to-canada-for-husbands-job-2025-10">living in Canada</a>.</p><p>I remember seeing people on the internet working remotely or starting businesses in places like <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/retirees-chiang-mai-thailand-retirement-abroad-2026-6">Chiang Mai, Thailand</a>. I started following some of them online and knew I wanted to find a way to do it, too.</p><p>At that time, I was working in corporate sales and ended up starting my own <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/how-to-start-furniture-repair-business-from-scratch-2021-2">furniture business</a> in Toronto. I hoped to scale it enough to manage remotely, but because it was a physical business, I had to be on-site.</p><p>I eventually sold my share to my business partner and got a job at a marketing software startup based in Toronto instead.</p><p>The company was fully remote and didn't have an office, so that's when I started traveling.</p>
      <aside class="callout-box headline-regular ignore-typography">
        <p>Have you relocated abroad — especially to Asia — for career opportunities, retirement, or lower living costs? We want to hear from you. Fill out this <a target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow" href="https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdxVL1zX0AV0FiTKnYB72xTcK5G4gxa8o5PwKsxTEwmgZJg1A/viewform">short form</a> to share your story.</p>
      </aside>
    <p>I didn't inform anyone at my company. A few months later, after a strong performance review, I finally told my boss that I'd been working from Peru.</p><p>He went, "Oh, OK, cool." And we never really talked about it after. I just kept working remotely and became a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/digital-nomads-looking-for-love-dating-mistakes-to-avoid-2024-9">full-time nomad</a>, traveling mostly through South America the next several years, visiting places like Argentina and Colombia.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a7d7b77e3df4d0cbe6857d1?format=jpeg" height="1108" width="1477" alt="The living room."><figcaption>He first learned about digital nomadism after seeing people online working remotely while traveling.<p class="copyright">Provided by Francis Cloutier.</p></figcaption></figure><p>Thailand had been on my radar since the beginning, but back then, I worried that if I hated it and wanted to come back, I'd be so far from home.</p><p>Then, about a year and a half ago, a friend <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/american-retiree-left-hawaii-moved-abroad-bangkok-thailand-2026-2">living in Bangkok</a> invited me over for a visit.</p><p>I'd worked evenings while traveling in Europe before, and figured I could handle working nights in Thailand for a few months.</p><h2 id="2781d249-671e-4061-ba9a-610e336f2f73" data-toc-id="2781d249-671e-4061-ba9a-610e336f2f73">Bangkok won me over</h2><p>I ended up falling in love with Bangkok. It was my <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/thailand-mistakes-visiting-bangkok-first-time-with-family-tips">first time in Asia</a>, and about a month in, I knew I wanted to spend more time here.</p><p>It's super convenient, and the public transit is fantastic. I go to nightclubs and don't have to constantly watch for pickpockets or worry about where I'll end up.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a7d7b75c78818eff7d2c7e7?format=jpeg" height="2168" width="2892" alt="The study."><figcaption>Cloutier spent several years traveling through South America before a friend&#39;s invitation brought him to Bangkok.<p class="copyright">Provided by Francis Cloutier.</p></figcaption></figure><p>As I settled into <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/american-single-mom-california-bangkok-thailand-daughter-affordable-slow-lifestyle-2026-1">life in Bangkok</a>, I found another reason to stay: I met my then-girlfriend at the bar where she worked as a bartender.</p><p>We got married, and in April, moved into a two-bedroom condo together in central Bangkok.</p><p>After nearly seven <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/emotional-cost-to-moving-abroad-nomadic-life-2026-7">years of nomadic living</a>, including my first months in Bangkok, hopping between Airbnb rentals, I wanted a place that felt more like home.</p><p>My priorities were a modern apartment on a fairly high floor, easy access to public transit, and at least two bedrooms so I could have a dedicated home office.</p><p>I've spent years working at kitchen tables on tiny chairs, so I now have a proper setup.</p><p>Rent is 30,000 Thai baht, or about $900, a month, and the building has a pool, gym, coworking space, and rooftop area that doubles as a viewing deck.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a7d7b76e3df4d0cbe6857d0?format=jpeg" height="2151" width="2868" alt="The bedroom."><figcaption>He met his now-wife in Bangkok, where they now live together in a two-bedroom condo.<p class="copyright">Provided by Francis Cloutier.</p></figcaption></figure><p>In Toronto, I was paying 1,350 Canadian dollars, or about $970, a month for a one-bedroom basement apartment outside the city.</p><h2 id="566afd83-549f-4575-9d57-1293e08b7392" data-toc-id="566afd83-549f-4575-9d57-1293e08b7392">Working US hours in Asia</h2><p id="566afd83-549f-4575-9d57-1293e08b7392">When most people in Bangkok are winding down for the day, I'm just getting to work.</p><p id="566afd83-549f-4575-9d57-1293e08b7392">My clients are based in North America, so I keep US Eastern business hours, which means I typically work from around 8 or 9 p.m. until 4 or 5 a.m. in Bangkok. I go to sleep as soon as I finish work. By the time I wake up, it's 2 or 3 p.m., so I still get some sunlight.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a7d7b76bd87410e364d1ec6?format=jpeg" height="1108" width="1477" alt="The kitchen."><figcaption>Rent is 30,000 Thai baht, or about $900, each month.<p class="copyright">Provided by Francis Cloutier.</p></figcaption></figure><p>I was always a night owl, and it also works out well because my partner is still a bartender, so she has the same schedule. She gets home around 3:30 a.m.</p><p>It helps that Bangkok is a city that never sleeps. Everything's available at pretty much any hour.</p><p>I have a general idea of my monthly expenses. I mostly eat out or order in, so I spend about $1,000 on food. Utilities and internet are another $200 or so, because we use quite a bit of air conditioning. My health insurance is about $50 a month.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a7d7b77c78818eff7d2c7e8?format=jpeg" height="893" width="1191" alt="The view from the apartment building."><figcaption>He said it&#39;s been easy to adjust to working nights because Bangkok is a city that never sleeps.<p class="copyright">Provided by Francis Cloutier.</p></figcaption></figure><p>For<strong> </strong>the lifestyle I live here, I would be living paycheck to paycheck in North America. My quality of life by pretty much every metric is higher than it was back there.</p><p>The only downside is the air quality in this city.</p><p>I don't think I'll ever <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-home-canada-living-abroad-friendships-changed-2026-5">move back to Canada</a>. I hate winter. I would prefer sweating in the tropical heat to snow and de-icing my car in the morning.</p><p>I usually go back once a year. I try to time my visits around Christmas or my mother's birthday so I can be there for those times.</p><p>My mom is getting older. I'm her only son, so if she needs me, I'm either going to have to move her to wherever I settle down or spend some time in Canada.</p><p>I'm not 100% sure yet what that will look like yet.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-to-bangkok-works-american-business-hours-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>Sam Altman says he's worried about AI being controlled by a few powerful players</title>
    <updated>2026-08-23T21:47:49Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/sam-altman-openai-risks-ai-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8b480f8a99fa493d60f442?format=jpeg" height="5464" width="8192" alt="CEO of OpenAI Sam Altman talks to reporters following a meeting with Senator Bernie Sanders (I-VT) at the Dirksen Senate Office building in Washington, DC on June 3, 2026."><figcaption>OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.<p class="copyright">Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the power of AI could become concentrated among a handful of players.</li><li>Altman said fears about AI safety could lead people to trade their liberty.</li><li>He said AI should instead empower individuals and fuel a boom in small businesses.</li></ul><p>OpenAI CEO <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/sam-altman">Sam Altman</a> says he worries that AI will one day be controlled by a handful of companies, models, or people, leaving the vast majority of consumers without a say in how the technology shapes the world.</p><p>"The right approach is to say we want people deeply in control of the future," Altman said on David Senra's podcast, which was released on Sunday. "Society and the models are going to co-evolve."</p><p>The other possibility Altman said he worries about is AI breaking free from its human handlers. Paradoxically, Altman said a fear of the latter possibility could lead to an actualization of the former.</p><p>"There are a lot of people who are so nervous about the magnitude of those risks and get so taken by that and feel a need to protect the world," he said. "Like, you know, 'we should trade off a lot of liberty for safety.'"</p><p>Altman was most likely thinking about Anthropic CEO <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/dario-amodei">Dario Amodei</a>.</p><p>Amodei has warned on podcasts, in essays, and in company blog posts, about the dangers posed by AI's rapid development. In a June essay, Amodei wrote that the company's <a target="_self" rel="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/dario-amodei-ai-warnings-mythos-fable-blocked-2026-6"><u>new Mythos models</u></a> present "very real risks" to cybersecurity, the financial sector, critical infrastructure, and national security.</p><p>Amodei has used those warnings to advocate for a greater government role in regulating AI. In Altman's view, that might be trading liberty for safety.</p><p>Anthropic was also the only major AI company last month not to sign a letter endorsing open-weight models, which allow developers to share, download, modify, and deploy AI models on their own infrastructure.</p><p>China has embraced the open-weight model, which has allowed it to keep up with Silicon Valley at a fraction of the cost. Some in the United States, including Nvidia, Meta, and Microsoft, have argued that America needs to do the same or risk ceding ground to its rival in the AI race.</p><p>OpenAI, though it has not released the source code of its frontier models, did release two <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/openai-gpt-oss-open-weight-llm-ai-model-2025-8">open-weight models</a> last year, gpt-oss-120b and gpt-oss-20b.</p><p>During the podcast, Altman also said AI leaders in the United States have failed to demonstrate to the public how the technology can give people greater autonomy over their lives.</p><p>"We are about to see the greatest boom in people starting smaller businesses than we have ever seen," he said. "I think AI is empowering that."</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/sam-altman-openai-risks-ai-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-08-23T21:38:35Z</published>
    <summary type="text">OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that fears about AI going off the rails could lead people to trade liberty for safety.</summary>

    <title>Nike is offering $4,000 in rent money to winners of an NYC race. In Manhattan, that might not be enough.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-23T20:05:03Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/nike-nyc-street-race-free-rent-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8b31ae4569a4ec219f94c7?format=jpeg" height="2763" width="4144" alt="A Nike logo sign is seen on a store in New York City, United States, on August 6, 2026."><figcaption>Nike is hosting a street race in New York City. The winners will get $4,000, or as the company puts it, a month&#39;s rent.<p class="copyright">Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Nike is offering two winners of a NYC street race $4,000, or as the company puts it, a month's rent.</li><li>The money, however, would fall short of Manhattan's $5,000 median market-rate rent.</li><li>The race comes as Mayor Zohran Mamdani pushes to make city housing more affordable.</li></ul><p>It might be possible to outrun your next rent payment — if you live with roommates.</p><p>Nike is offering a unique — and highly relevant — prize to two winners of a street race in New York City on August 29: "1 month of free rent."</p><p>"Step to the starting line on Orchard Street for a chance to win one month of rent paid," the company says.</p><p>Participants, who will be chosen by a random drawing, will race in a series of 100-meter dashes, advancing through an undisclosed number of heats before racing in a final round.</p><p>At the end of it all, the two fastest participants will each earn up to $4,000, which Nike is marketing as enough for a month's rent.</p><p>For many New Yorkers, though, that might not cover it.</p><p>The <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/manhattan-apartment-rent-increase-inventory-drops-zohran-mamdani-2026-8">median Manhattan rental price</a> for a market-rate apartment, where the race is set to occur, soared to $5,000 last month, according to an August report from The Real Deal and appraisal firm Samuel Miller.</p><p>Should the winners of the races hail from Queens or Brooklyn, the $4,000 prize will likely be enough, but not by much. According to data from Apartments.com, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Queens is $3,605. In Brooklyn, it's $3,082.</p><p>Mayor Zohran Mamdani has made lowering the <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/category/cost-of-the-city">city's astronomical housing costs</a> a centerpiece of his administration. His signature rent freeze for roughly 1 million rent-stabilized apartments takes effect this fall, while City Hall is pursuing a broader plan to build and preserve 200,000 affordable homes over the next decade.</p><p>Representatives for Mamdani did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday.</p><p>The race comes as <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/nike-comeback-stock-shoes-retail-sales-sports-focus-2026-4">Nike tries to recapture</a> some of the cultural cachet it's lost in recent years. CEO Elliott Hill, a Nike veteran who returned to lead the company in 2024, has been working to refocus the brand on sports, rebuild relationships with retailers, and revive product innovation after years of losing ground to competitors like Hoka and On.</p><p>The turnaround has shown signs of progress in North America, but it's been slow going. Nike's shares remain well below their 2021 peak, while weakness in China and other challenges continue to weigh on the company.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/nike-nyc-street-race-free-rent-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-08-23T19:45:07Z</published>
    <summary type="text">Four grand wouldn't cover a month's rent for most residents of Manhattan these days. In Brooklyn and Queens? Just barely.</summary>

    <title>Hugging Face has been fielding M&A interest for a deal worth at least $13 billion</title>
    <updated>2026-08-23T21:10:03Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/hugging-face-could-be-acquired-13-billion-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a60930254f987526177814a?format=jpeg" height="2662" width="4000" alt="clement delangue, ceo of hugging face, sits in front of a camera"><figcaption>Clement Delangue, co-founder and chief executive officer of Hugging Face.<p class="copyright">Bloomberg/Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>AI developer startup Hugging Face has been in talks to be acquired for at least $13 billion.</li><li>Hugging Face allows developers to publish, share, and download various AI models.</li><li>The potential interest comes as Stripe acquired OpenRouter for a deal worth around $8 billion.</li></ul><p>The AI industry's next blockbuster acquisition may not be another model maker.</p><p><a target="_blank" class="" href="https://huggingface.co/">Hugging Face,</a> <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/top-ai-models-usage-data-hugging-face-2026-8">whose platform helps developers</a> discover, share, and build AI models, has been exploring a sale that could value the company at $13 billion or more.</p><p>The startup has been working with a bank to evaluate bidders' interest, and no deal has been reached yet, according to people familiar with the matter.</p><p>Hugging Face is a platform where developers publish, share, and download various AI models. The talks show how valuable AI developer platforms have become as the industry matures. The startup was last valued at $4.5 billion in 2023, per PitchBook. Investors include Lux Capital, Addition, and Salesforce Ventures.</p><p>Hugging Face was founded in 2016 by French entrepreneurs Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond, and Thomas Wolf.</p><p>Rather than competing to build the next frontier model, companies like Hugging Face have become essential for developers who build with AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and others.</p><p>Following Stripe's <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/stripe-is-finalizing-8b-openrouter-purchase-investors-could-gain-2026-8">agreement to buy </a><a target="_self" rel="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/ai-routing-startups-openrouter-concentrate-funding-boom-2026-6"><u>AI model marketplace startup </u></a><a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/stripe-is-finalizing-8b-openrouter-purchase-investors-could-gain-2026-8">OpenRouter</a> for around $8 billion, interest in Hugging Face suggests investors are increasingly willing to pay premium prices for companies at the center of the AI ecosystem even if they aren't building the models themselves.</p><p>Hugging Face <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/smart-people-react-openai-hugging-face-hacking-cybersecurity-incident-2026-7">recently found</a> itself at the center of an unusual security incident after OpenAI disclosed that one of its AI agents escaped a controlled cybersecurity test, accessed the internet, and breached Hugging Face while attempting to solve the challenge.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/hugging-face-could-be-acquired-13-billion-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>Texas Gov. Greg Abbott says data centers deserve the backlash they're getting: 'They basically dug their own grave'</title>
    <updated>2026-08-23T16:42:33Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/greg-abbott-texas-data-centers-backlash-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8b001f1d1a1d028ba121af?format=jpeg" height="5504" width="8256" alt="Greg Abbott"><figcaption>Gov. Greg Abbott introduced new standards around data centers in Texas after community backlash.<p class="copyright">Brandon Bell/Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Texas Gov. Greg Abbott said the backlash data centers are getting from Americans is deserved.</li><li>Abbott, who earlier supported data center development in the state, has since changed his tune.</li><li>Politicians are navigating the data center debate ahead of the November midterm elections.</li></ul><p>The AI industry is reaping what it sows, as far as Texas Gov. Greg Abbott is concerned.</p><p>Abbott said the sharp criticism Americans are lobbing at <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/why-everyone-hates-data-center-ai-industry-debate-2026-8">AI data centers</a> is well-earned during an interview on ABC's "This Week" on Sunday.</p><p>"They basically dug their own grave for the problem that's been caused for them, and that's why they got the backlash they deserve," Abbott said.</p><p>Tech companies rely on data centers to power their AI products, but their messaging around them has fallen flat. All across the country, Americans are rallying to <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/data-center-industry-response-growing-pushback-regulation-2026-4">fight against AI data centers</a>, which can cost billions to build and span hundreds of acres. Many are concerned about how the sprawling facilities will affect the environment, utility prices, water resources, and noise levels, to name a few. Some just generally don't like AI.</p><p>Critics have crowded local planning meetings, created petitions, staged protests, and even taken legal action to stop construction. Surveys conducted by The Pew Research Center and Gallup this year said a large chunk of Americans are opposed to living near an AI data center.</p><p>"Seven in 10 Americans oppose constructing data centers for artificial intelligence in their local area, including nearly half, 48%, who are strongly opposed," the Gallup survey said.</p><p>That's a tricky reality for conservative politicians like Abbott, who must balance the <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/ai-data-center-backlash-midterm-elections-voters-2026-8">will of his voters</a> and that of <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/donald-trump">President Donald Trump</a> ahead of the midterm elections. The Trump administration has gone all in on AI, including accelerating federal permitting and supporting the <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/oracle-openai-stargate-loans-jpmorgan-diminishing-interest-debt-2026-1">$500 billion Stargate Project</a>, an ambitious plan led by OpenAI and Oracle to build hyperscale data centers across the country.</p><p>Abbott was initially an ardent supporter of AI data center projects in Texas for their economic benefit. The giant server warehouses can generate jobs during construction and provide tax windfalls to local communities. However, Texans from Abilene to Sulphur Springs have taken hard stances against them, forcing Abbott to change his tune.</p><p>Abbott has introduced <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/texas-governor-proposes-new-data-center-regulations-2026-6">new standards for AI</a> data center projects in Texas, including instructing the state's utility commission and electrical grid operator to protect residents from infrastructure costs. He's also suggested a ban on data center developments in rural Texas, and that projects must undergo an audit before moving forward.</p><p>Abbott said earlier this month that his administration had halted some 1,800 AI data center projects in the state.</p><p>During the ABC interview, Abbott shared a few theories about why data centers are facing so much resistance, including the speed at which they are being built and brought online. The other is that data center developers aren't gaining local residents' support before pursuing projects.</p><p>"Gaining the support of people in local communities is essential," Abbott said.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/greg-abbott-texas-data-centers-backlash-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-08-23T16:42:33Z</published>
    <summary type="text">Gov. Greg Abbott initially supported expanding AI data center infrastructure in Texas, but backlash from local residents caused him to change course.</summary>

    <title>I'm 70 and raising my 7-year-old grandson. I have faith everything will work out, but I may never retire.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-23T16:00:13Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/grandmother-adopted-grandson-cant-retire-childcare-cost-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a889f181d1a1d028ba11d7a?format=jpeg" height="1350" width="1800" alt="Ruth Olinger (center) has raised dozens of foster children and is now parenting her grandson."><figcaption>Ruth Olinger (center) has raised dozens of foster children and is now parenting her grandson.<p class="copyright">Ruth Olinger</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Ruth Olinger, 70, is raising her grandson in Florida, highlighting the challenges of grandparenting.</li><li>Olinger, who fostered 51 children, faces financial strain after five-figure costs.</li><li>Olinger said that while they don't have everything they want, they have everything they need.</li></ul><p><em>This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Ruth Olinger, 70, who is </em><a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/grandparents-raising-grandchildren-retirement-caregiving-costs-vacations-2026-7"><em>raising her grandson</em></a><em> on her own in Lakeland, Florida. Olinger had earlier fostered dozens of children and did mission work. Now, Olinger said she can't retire and paid over $10,000 for her son's day care. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.</em></p><p>I was <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/grandparents-raising-grandchildren-retirement-foster-care-aging-insurance-financial-instability-2026-5">raised by my grandparents</a>. My grandmother had rheumatoid arthritis, so my grandfather did the cooking and cleaning. She was bedridden for 16 years, and I would take care of her. He had a stroke one day, and he was never the same. We were then placed in <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/single-foster-mom-adoption-journey-2024-4">foster care</a> when I was 8, and my brother was 10. We were separated after three months.</p><p>My brother was in several different homes and got emancipated at 16. I was in 10 homes, so I called 10 different parents "mom" and "dad." I always felt like I wasn't good enough and wondered if I was lovable.</p><p>I went to college at 17 and graduated early. I got married at 18 because I had nowhere else to go. My grandparents had died. I had two sons, and at the age of 28, I met my biological father.</p><p>I knew I wanted to give back in some way, so I fostered 51 children over the years, all of which were during my single years. I didn't want anybody to feel less than. The harder they were to love, the better I liked them. They all needed to be loved and feel secure in their environment.</p>
      <aside class="callout-box headline-regular ignore-typography">
        <p>Business Insider wants to hear from grandparents <strong>caring for their grandchildren</strong> and older Americans caring for younger loved ones. <strong>Share your story by filling out this </strong><a target="_blank" rel=" nofollow" class="" href="https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSc3B3DqRcKUfGoxcUcf_oEPQOwyzJf0I-jL15r4T_XT_ZOs1Q/viewform?usp=preview"><strong>quick form</strong></a><strong>.</strong></p>
      </aside>
    <p>I got divorced and remarried after 15 years. I had a son 18 years after my last son. Then, I <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/college-students-adopted-first-child-2025-4">adopted our daughter</a>. A few years ago, I adopted my grandson, and I now call him my son. At age 70, I have five children. The oldest is 48, and the youngest, Atlas, is 7.</p><h2 id="ab222f9d-5c67-4002-bd03-357c17361028" data-toc-id="ab222f9d-5c67-4002-bd03-357c17361028"><strong>I've never really worried about finances.</strong></h2><p>I have faith that everything will work out. I've worked three jobs at one time. I've mowed grass with one son sitting on my lap and the other holding onto the back of the lawnmower. I mowed four acres of land for $10, and that gave us milk for the week. I worked in insurance and banking, but I fell in love with mission work and helping other people. At one time, I was working 90 hours a week.</p><p>There are givers and takers in the world, and I'm a giver. I raised millions to build a center for homeless women and children. I did mission work in Belgium, Italy, Scotland, Ireland, West Africa, and Kenya. I helped operate two orphanages. I recently gave clothes to a single mom who didn't have.</p><p>I also cared for my natural mother, who did not raise me, as well as my best friend. I <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/built-house-mom-with-dementia-nursing-home-costs-2026-8">built my house</a> so that we would have enough room for all of us to be together. I always considered it a privilege to be here with them and help them through tough times.</p><h2 id="92cbf6be-0e17-4896-be3c-9bd653e36e75" data-toc-id="92cbf6be-0e17-4896-be3c-9bd653e36e75"><strong>I adopted my grandson.</strong></h2><p>I've cared for my youngest pretty much since he was born. His mother, my daughter, had him for over a year, but it wasn't working out, so they allowed me to adopt him. He's absolutely perfect, and he adds so much to my life. He's eager, interested, and curious. Of course, he has some <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/common-subtle-signs-of-cancer-doctor-2026-3">health issues</a> and loses his temper from time to time. But he is definitely a blessing.</p><p>He was diagnosed with a disease that was time-consuming to get him the diagnosis, and it <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/self-made-millionaire-steps-to-hitting-financial-freedom-early-retirement-2026-1">hit my finances</a> because I lost days of work. It takes a special person to love that child, tuck them in bed every night, and hold them when they're hurting.</p><p>My daughter and I didn't talk for about two and a half years, but we're very close now. She has many gifts and talents. Sometimes, though, you get in the wrong relationship.</p><h2 id="5fe8db1a-e6ad-4420-ae5d-1821fd091cdd" data-toc-id="5fe8db1a-e6ad-4420-ae5d-1821fd091cdd"><strong>I've tried not to let my age get in the way of anything.</strong></h2><p>I'm able to walk and care for myself. I still climb into the playground and play with Atlas. We've camped outside in tents. There is plenty I can't do that I did with my older children. I let him race up and down the driveway, which I don't do.</p><p>In some ways, I'm more patient with him because of my experience <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/grandparents-raising-grandchildren-adoption-retirement-aging-economy-financial-instability-2026-6">raising children</a> and being older. In other ways, I'm less patient because, as you get older, there is a point where you can be less patient, but the quality is still the same. We sit down and talk about earning things because of responsibility. I do a lot more homework with him than I did with my other kids when they were in school. He's dyslexic, which can be a challenge, but he's maturing.</p><p>During the summer, I take him swimming. I think he's part fish because he wants to stay in all the time. He loves to ride his bike and watch TV.</p><p>I don't fit in with younger people raising young children, and I also don't fit in with the senior groups because they don't have to hire babysitters for outings.</p><h2 id="89f49103-9c93-41fb-af19-c09d09e808af" data-toc-id="89f49103-9c93-41fb-af19-c09d09e808af"><strong>My weeks are usually packed.</strong></h2><p>I work at a car dealership as an officer manager. I do a bit of everything, and I enjoy the challenge of helping people with financial or legal aspects. When he's asleep, I do my work in Kenya from abroad. I take off Saturdays to take him to fun places.</p><p>The biggest challenge for grandparents, I believe, is <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/working-mom-spends-20k-year-childcare-nyc-makes-sacrifices-2025-12">day care</a> and <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/disney-plans-employee-stock-purchase-program-health-insurance-plan-changes-2026-8">health insurance</a>. The advantage of adoption is that the state helps you with health insurance, but I've paid $10,400 a year for day care, which will blow your socks off when you weren't expecting that. I paid less than that when I had two kids.</p><p>Times have changed, and the grocery store gives me sticker shock. I spent $150 on my last grocery bill. I would much prefer to be sitting where nobody can see me and pay others' checks, but I don't have that luxury.</p><h2 id="0914136c-1a30-4f30-83a6-8bd8c6b6bb75" data-toc-id="0914136c-1a30-4f30-83a6-8bd8c6b6bb75"><strong>I'm not rich by any means, and we don't have everything that we want.</strong></h2><p>We do have what we need. We can supplement if we're running short. We can have egg sandwiches and grilled cheese instead of steak and lobster.</p><p>My concern is that my <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/90-still-work-retirement-social-security-job-training-lower-income-2025-7">Social Security</a> is $1,500 a month. Who can live on that? Add on the county property tax, which is $4,500 a year, and homeowner's insurance at $3,800 a year. That's a lot of money. I have my budget written out, and I pay my bills upfront. I'm pretty savvy when it comes to saving.</p><p>I will have to work until I step into my casket because I want my son to have what he needs. I've been asked to serve as a director of some local foundations because they know my background.</p><p>He's not going to have the best part of me because I'm getting older. You have to have hope and work as hard as you can. I don't want to be an absent parent, and I want to make sure that he has some advantages when I'm not there.</p><p>However, I don't want him to be handicapped by thinking that I'm going to give him everything. I want him to be able to stand on his own two feet and be whatever he wants to be.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/grandmother-adopted-grandson-cant-retire-childcare-cost-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-08-23T15:31:02Z</published>

    <title>I chose community college to save money. Now Yale is giving me a full ride.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-23T13:58:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/rio-brazil-community-college-yale-full-ride-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a847fa57e0482203ed171fe?format=jpeg" height="2018" width="2690" alt="Young man holding acceptance to Yale"><figcaption>Thalles de Souza moved from Brazil to the US as a child and was just accepted to Yale.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Thalles de Souza</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Thalles de Souza grew up surrounded by shootings and gang violence in Rio de Janeiro.</li><li>His single mother secretly saved money to move her children to the US.</li><li>After attending community college, he was accepted to Yale with a full-ride scholarship.</li></ul><p><em>This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Thalles de Souza. It has been edited for length and clarity.</em></p><p>In March 2016, on a Sunday morning, police entered my house, shouting and shooting. At only 13, I woke up screaming, not sure of what was happening. When I walked into the kitchen, I was nearly shot. Turns out, the police were looking for a family member of ours.</p><p>Shootings were common where I lived in Vila Kennedy, a community in Bangu, in <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/traveled-60-countries-chose-where-live-relocate-2024-11">Rio de Janeiro</a>. I witnessed so many deaths — countless deaths.</p><p>I lived there with my mom, a <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/love-being-single-mom-parent-how-i-want-2025-4">single mom</a>, and my three older siblings. My mom had always done what she could to protect us, given what she experienced as a child. After her parents died when she was 10, she became homeless. By 19, she had four children. She did what she could to keep us safe, but she couldn't hide what we saw in our community when we walked out the front door.</p><h2 id="153ffd5b-5412-405a-97df-5ceb4ed59262" data-toc-id="153ffd5b-5412-405a-97df-5ceb4ed59262">My mom decided to move us to the US</h2><p>There were a lot of gangs and so much corruption. Every day, people were killed. It was a normal occurrence to be playing soccer with my friends, right next to dead bodies lying in the street. I learned to navigate life in these spaces surrounded by danger, but it was normal — it was my reality.</p><p>On that Sunday in March 2016, my mom decided she had to get out to keep her children safe.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a85f9de7e0482203ed17afb?format=jpeg" height="3044" width="4096" alt="Mom and son"><figcaption>Thalles de Souza&#39;s mom moved her family to the US.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Thalles de Souza</p></figcaption></figure><p>She had quietly been saving small amounts of money, taking out loans, and applying for our visas so that we could travel to the US. She kept it quiet to make sure no one got in the way of her plan.</p><p>Three months after the shooting in our house, we <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-closer-kids-grandkids-regrets-moved-back-2026-6">moved to Cape Cod</a>, Massachusetts, and we never left. It became our home, our new community.</p><h2 id="76b4501a-b2dc-47ca-b100-e4f28af4c6d3" data-toc-id="76b4501a-b2dc-47ca-b100-e4f28af4c6d3">I went to community college to save money</h2><p>After <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/youngest-graduating-high-school-marking-end-motherhood-2026-6">graduating from high school</a>, I attended our local community college to save money and decide what college I would transfer to later.</p><p>In <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/more-students-should-consider-community-college-benefits-2025-9">community college</a>, I worked hard. I had perfect grades, became a member of the Massachusetts Board of Higher Education, participated in clubs, served as student body president for two years, and served the community I lived in, wanting to give back to the people who had welcomed my family.</p><p>Last year, I started looking for which college I was going to transfer to. I knew Yale had produced some of the best lawyers and judges — what I hoped to become — so I went for a visit.</p><h2 id="76d3c4e2-6247-4cb2-9674-b28eed4ff49b" data-toc-id="76d3c4e2-6247-4cb2-9674-b28eed4ff49b">I applied to Yale, thinking I wouldn't get in</h2><p>When I got out of my car, I said to myself that this place wasn't the kind of place that would accept someone like me. But I applied anyway. I knew there was only a 1.3% acceptance rate, but I had to try.</p><p>When I saw I had an email from the admissions office, I called my mom and older sister into the room with me to find out the result.</p><p>I got in. <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/student-wrote-about-mom-college-apps-yale-and-stanford-2025-11">I got into Yale</a>, one of the most prestigious universities in the world. Not just that — I had a 100% full-ride scholarship.</p><p>I still can't believe it, even though I'm starting in September.</p><p>Where I came from didn't determine where I could go. I might have started as just another unlikely statistic in society's eyes, but that isn't what I'll become.</p><p>On a visit to the campus a few weeks ago, my mom looked at me and said how amazing all of this was. She's so happy. She tells everyone. She sacrificed her entire life to get her children safe. And the result was far better than she could have imagined.</p><p>I'm so glad I've been able to give her the gift of knowing her sacrifice wasn't for nothing — it was all worth it.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/rio-brazil-community-college-yale-full-ride-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-08-23T13:58:01Z</published>
    <summary type="text">After immigrating from Brazil, Thalles de Souza attended community college to save money. He beat long odds to transfer to Yale with a full scholarship.</summary>

    <title>My 90-year-old dad didn't want caregivers in his home. He ended up gaining friends.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-23T13:52:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/elderly-parents-accepting-home-care-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a86f6ab0b0f848e0c30780b?format=jpeg" height="1200" width="1600" alt="A middle-aged woman is sitting on a bench with her father."><figcaption>The author with her 90-year-old father.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of the author</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>My 90-year-old father's needs have changed as his health has declined.</li><li>My sister had been his primary caregiver, but our family required extra help.</li><li>Dad hired male carers who take turns to attend to him. It's worked out extraordinarily well.</li></ul><p>My mother and father, ages 95 and 90, respectively, are proud to still live in their own home.</p><p>They enjoy a peaceful lifestyle that revolves around simple meals, afternoon trips into the <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/cotswolds-worth-visiting-english-rural-day-trips-london-better-touristy-2025-9">English countryside</a>, and reading the newspaper.</p><p>However, their health has inevitably declined. Dad has had a particularly hard year so far after a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/what-are-the-signs-of-a-heart-attack">heart attack </a>in January. The condition affected his mobility, making it difficult for him to take a shower, get in and out of bed, and move without a walker.</p><p>My sister, 61, who retired early from her job <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/how-being-a-nurse-has-changed-2019-4">as a nurse</a> to care for my parents, and I became increasingly worried.</p>
      
      <aside class="callout-box headline-regular ignore-typography">
        
        <p><strong>What is your situation regarding long-term care for yourself or your loved ones? To share your story with a Business Insider reporter, please fill out this </strong><a target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow" href="https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdg4AoiQ9q9GU2sU75z7cCrHvjt0JnM_0Nf34JYn_1DpF3w6A/viewform?usp=dialog"><strong>quick form</strong></a><strong>.</strong></p>
      
      </aside>
    
    <p>She could do things like cooking and laundry relatively smoothly, but lifting Dad was becoming a problem. She weighed less than 120 pounds, and her back was under strain.</p><p>It was a difficult conversation, but it had to happen. "Jane and I think it's time to bring in some outside help," my sister told our parents. The carers could be very part-time, she suggested, and swing by as needed.</p><p>Dad looked at his hands. Mom wiped away a tear. They are private people. Neither wanted strangers in the house.</p><h2 id="80bde84f-7d10-4919-b1e7-adc54072e1f7" data-toc-id="80bde84f-7d10-4919-b1e7-adc54072e1f7">We contacted eldercare agencies</h2><p>Still, they promised to give the matter some thought. They talked things through with my aunt, my mom's best friend, and she advised them to give it a shot. They could always change their minds.</p><p>My sister contacted several <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/long-term-care-costs-growing-problem-for-americans-2026-8">eldercare agencies</a> in the town. She asked friends for recommendations and found what seemed like a decent choice. To our surprise, there was no waiting list. Dad's carers could start almost immediately.</p><p>Their appointment coincided with my visiting the UK from New York in July, while my sister flew to see her adult son <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moving-to-canada-from-us-cost-of-living-higher-happier-2025-3">in Canada</a>. The plan was for me to replace her as the main caregiver for two weeks, with support from the agency's staff.</p><h2 id="78aa08fd-dd6e-47de-9b52-fa38b0dc6075" data-toc-id="78aa08fd-dd6e-47de-9b52-fa38b0dc6075">Dad needed help with washing and dressing</h2><p>Mom, Dad, and I were nervous when Jonathan, the first of the two carers, showed up for his first shift. We feared the meeting might be awkward.</p><p>It was quite the opposite. Jonathan arrived with a beaming smile and literally rolled up his sleeves to get on with the job. He cracked jokes as he escorted Dad to the bathroom.</p><p>He helped him get washed and dressed before sitting him down for breakfast. His manner was bright and breezy.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a871de24569a4ec219f869f?format=jpeg" height="2268" width="3024" alt="A woman pushing an older man in a wheelchair."><figcaption>The author with her father during her recent visit to the UK.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of the author</p></figcaption></figure><p>Dad, a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/boomer-retiring-soon-ready-to-do-all-the-things-2024-5">retired journalist</a>, has an endless curiosity about people. It wasn't long before he was asking Jonathan questions about his family, career, and taste in sports.</p><p>They chatted away like friends. Within an hour, Dad knew all about Jonathan's wife, two kids, and parents, who lived in Nigeria, his home country.</p><h2 id="3eb71435-1d6b-441c-a5af-77fe8bf511ed" data-toc-id="3eb71435-1d6b-441c-a5af-77fe8bf511ed">Mom overcame her reticence</h2><p>Equally, Dad grilled Jonathan's colleague, Junior, originally from Ghana, who worked about half the shifts. While less gregarious than Jonathan, he was a kind, thoughtful man.</p><p>He treated my father with respect and admiration. Caring for seniors isn't easy, but he was clearly suited to the role.</p><p>The days went by, and Dad couldn't say enough good things about both carers. Mom overcame her reticence and greeted them cheerfully at the door each morning and evening.</p><p>"Your dad likes to have other men around to talk to," she told my sister and me. He'd been outnumbered by women in the house for years, and it was a pleasant change.</p><h2 id="4ee6b6e6-a508-4a90-b245-eed48bea6b31" data-toc-id="4ee6b6e6-a508-4a90-b245-eed48bea6b31">My dad bonded with his aide over music</h2><p>One of the most delightful things to have come out of the arrangement was the bond that Dad forged with Junior <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/reference/benefits-of-music">over music</a>.</p><p>Their routine includes listening to jazz on Junior's <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/reference/how-to-update-spotify">Spotify app</a> during his working hours. He is 65 years younger than my father, but they both sing along to the grainy-sounding tunes from the 1930s and 40s.</p><p>It's been almost two months since the carers entered my parents' lives. Everyone agrees that it was the right decision, given the circumstances.</p><p>More than that, Jonathan and Junior have shown us that our folks are in the best possible hands.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/elderly-parents-accepting-home-care-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-08-23T13:52:01Z</published>
    <summary type="text">My aging parents wanted to remain independent and resisted home care. Their new aides quickly became a welcome part of their lives.</summary>

    <title>I booked a $200 flight to Panama on a whim, then decided to move there. I found the community I was missing in the US.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-23T12:23:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/cheap-flight-panama-city-moved-from-atlanta-community-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a85d3290b0f848e0c30729c?format=jpeg" height="1736" width="1320" alt="Person in a navy outfit stands barefoot on a high balcony overlooking blue water and a distant skyline."><figcaption>Chrysten Crockett moved from Atlanta to Panama City and said she&#39;s staying for good.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Chrysten Crockett.</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Chrysten Crockett visited Panama during a trip to Latin America and fell in love with the country.</li><li>She thinks Panama is more welcoming than the US and has a stronger sense of community.</li><li>Crockett will still travel the world, but Panama has become her permanent home base.</li></ul><p><em>This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Chrysten Crockett, a Cleveland native who moved from Atlanta to Panama City. Crockett, 36, owns a content marketing agency that she now runs from Panama. The following has been edited for length and clarity.</em></p><p>I have no kids and I am not married, so I decided to <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/solo-trips-instead-of-having-kids-marriage-90-countries-2025-7">take a leap and travel</a>. I was like, "Let me try this travel thing out while I can."</p><p>I've always been nomadic in a way; I went from Ohio to New York to Charlotte to Atlanta. Then I thought, let's try out another country this time. I didn't really know where I wanted to live; I just knew I wanted to move.</p><p>I had a list of countries I wanted to check out. Costa Rica was on the list, along with Brazil, Colombia, and others.</p><p>Then I met someone who knew I was going to be traveling and they said, "Have you ever <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/retired-american-couple-moved-panama-unexpected-passion-writing-social-groups-2026-2">considered Panama?</a>" I said, no, actually, I haven't. I went home that night, looked up Panama City, and I was like, "Oh wow, it's a big city. I didn't know that. Let me look up flights."</p><p>Flights from Atlanta were around $200 one-way. I booked a flight that night.</p><p>Panama was the first stop on my trip, and when I got there, I fell in love. I was blown away because I had never been, and I didn't know much about the country. It opened up an opportunity to <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-remote-town-pacific-coast-surprises-santa-catalina-panama-2025">explore a new place</a> — and it's also very beautiful.</p><p>So it was an easy yes when I got here. When I got off the flight, I was like, "Oh my gosh, I love this place already. I can live here."</p><p>After Panama, I explored a little bit more of Latin America, but nothing hit like Panama, so I came back.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a85d32885cca0a87cd8aa15?format=jpeg" height="1963" width="1320" alt="Person in a green dress sits at a balcony table overlooking a waterfront city skyline."><figcaption>Crockett visited Panama for the first time on a trip to Latin America.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Chrysten Crockett.</p></figcaption></figure><p><a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/panama-8-day-visit-3-different-countries-2024-8">My first time in Panama</a> after taking that leap was December 2024, and my actual move and the legal process of becoming a resident started this year, in March 2026.</p><p>When people ask, "Why?" I always ask them, "Why not? What made <em>you</em> say, 'I'm going to live <em>here</em> for the rest of my life?'"</p><p>My motivation for moving out of the US was that I truly don't have a reason to go back. That can sound a bit cold, because I do miss my <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-to-small-town-different-country-struggled-panama-2025-12">family and my friends</a>, but they can visit.</p><h2 id="3a506ce7-c09c-4f47-88ef-1dd937079e39" data-toc-id="3a506ce7-c09c-4f47-88ef-1dd937079e39">I didn't bring much with me from the US — and things are cheaper here</h2><p>When I left Atlanta, I put all of my stuff in storage. I've mastered the art of detachment, so I didn't bring anything with me when I left but my two suitcases.</p><p>So it was very easy to transition. Luckily, in Panama, a lot of apartments are fully furnished, so it's not like I had to ship furniture or ship a car — I sold my car.</p><p>A lot of people here don't have a lot, and there are plenty of people here who do, so the gap is pretty big.</p><p>The first thing I noticed was groceries. In the US, I could go to a major grocery chain and spend $500 and not even have a week's worth of food. Here, I can spend $70 to $80 and have a full week of food, with some left over.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a85d32985cca0a87cd8aa17?format=jpeg" height="1720" width="1320" alt="A person seated in a restaurant booth bites into fried food with multiple plates of food on the table."><figcaption>Crockett said she gets a lot more for her rent in Panama City than in the US.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Chrysten Crockett.</p></figcaption></figure><p>Rent is going to vary depending on how you like to live. If I were to rent the apartment that I have now in Atlanta, it would easily cost me $4,000 to $5,000 a month, versus here it's $2,050 a month. Granted, it's a one-bedroom, and I live in one of the most expensive buildings in Panama.</p><p>There are plenty of other places in Panama where you can live for $1,000 a month. Some people are paying $300 for a mortgage for a three-bedroom home in the city. So you have access to plenty of options here, and that's what makes it special and unique.</p><h2 id="17675f2f-20ee-4e5d-86e2-5ebc4c5b1b61" data-toc-id="17675f2f-20ee-4e5d-86e2-5ebc4c5b1b61">The energy in Panama is invigorating</h2><p>There's so much culture here, and when I say that, I don't just mean in terms of race or ethnicity. I mean that Panama's culture is about relationships and community.</p><p>The energy is high because people are helping each other. It's like, "How can I scratch your back and you can scratch mine?" — but not just from a transactional standpoint; people truly want to help you.</p><p>If you're lost and need somewhere to go, people will stop in the middle of the street to ask if you're OK or hungry. It's a very unified environment, which feels very good. And although I love being a US citizen and being from the US, I miss that feeling.</p><p>Panama has the warmth and humility that I think the US has lost along the way, because people are more focused on surviving, making money, and buying. I think we've lost a little bit of our humility and our compassion as a result.</p><p>Yes, people work in Panama and they work hard — and there are people who maybe aren't doing so well, but that's everywhere — but you don't feel the energy of stress here. And I like that.</p><p>When you get to Panama, it is so warm and welcoming. Go to a playground, and there are kids running around without their parents around, without fear that the kids are going to get kidnapped or something's going to happen to them. It feels safe.</p><p>As a solo woman traveler, when I first got here, I didn't know what the safety situation would be like. I would look around my environment, and I would see women at night walking their dogs, looking down at their phones, and I'm like, "OK, it must be pretty safe here." As I grew to learn the city, I found that to be true.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a85d32885cca0a87cd8aa16?format=jpeg" height="851" width="1320" alt="Person in a green top seated at a restaurant table with red plates, glassware, and tropical plants behind them."><figcaption>Crockett said she feels safer and more welcomed in Panama than in the US.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Chrysten Crockett.</p></figcaption></figure><p>When you're in an environment where you know harm isn't lurking around the corner, it feels very peaceful.</p><p>Now that I have established this as a home base, I can continue my travels. But Panama is definitely where I see myself long-term.</p><p>To be able to come back and call this place home for me is really special, and I think that's how a lot of people who relocate here feel. </p><p>I get the same or similar answers from people who I have met along the way, regardless of whether they <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/moved-to-panama-from-us-for-retirement-cost-pros-cons-2025-4">moved to Panama from the US</a>, Canada, Australia, or Guam. It doesn't matter. Everyone who comes here to live here feels that similar warmth and energy of a country that truly makes you feel the love. </p><p>So, Panama, I'm here to stay.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/cheap-flight-panama-city-moved-from-atlanta-community-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
