    <title>I created a viral AI watermark remover. I wasn't ready for all the attention.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-23T11:32:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/created-viral-ai-watermark-remover-after-anthropics-announcement-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8735688a99fa493d60e703?format=jpeg" height="960" width="1280" alt="Bald person with a beard wearing a dark blazer poses against a green studio backdrop."><figcaption>Guillaume Meyer created a viral AI watermark remover.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Guillaume Meyer</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Guillaume Meyer created "Watermarks Remover" after Anthropic's AI watermark announcement.</li><li>Meyer's open-source project gained viral attention after he published the tool online.</li><li>He believes AI watermarks create more problems than they solve, but he supports content attribution.</li></ul><p><em>This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Guillaume Meyer, a Paris-based tech founder and creator of a viral open-source project "Watermarks Remover," which he made in response to </em><a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/anthropic-watermarking-feature-stops-undetected-ai-generated-writing-2026-8"><em>Anthropic's AI watermark announcement</em></a><em>. His words have been edited for length and clarity.</em></p><p>I'm an entrepreneur, and I've been in the tech industry for over 20 years.</p><p>Last week, Anthropic announced it would add an <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/anthropic-claude-text-watermark-concerns-tech-community-answers-2026-8">invisible AI watermark</a>. I knew other vendors, like Gemini, were already doing this, and out of curiosity, I started researching what AI watermarking is and how it works.</p><p>I had the idea to build a tool to see if I could remove the invisible watermark. A few hours later, I published the first version of my <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/ai-watermark-remover-tools-anthropic-2026-8">watermark remover</a> on GitHub.</p><p>After my second X post about the project on August 11, it blew up, and I got over 2 million impressions. I later discovered that it went viral on LinkedIn and other social networks, too.</p><p>I had to create new accounts just to learn about what people were saying about it.</p><p>I was not ready for the attention.</p><h2 id="18b91803-a9ef-4d2e-af2c-b013f20a196b" data-toc-id="18b91803-a9ef-4d2e-af2c-b013f20a196b">Anthropic's version of AI watermarks generates more problems than they solve</h2><p>From a practical standpoint, one of the core issues is that <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/john-gruber-claude-watermark-perversion-offensive-ai-2026-8">the AI watermark technique</a> that Anthropic is using relies on statistical analysis. This means it can generate false positives and have human victims. Researchers will publish papers labeled with the watermark, even if they use AI to change just one line at the end of a 10-page paper. It could be a nightmare for trust.</p><p>The best example I can give of this being problematic is that I'm not a native English speaker. All day, I use Grammarly to proofread what I'm writing, spell-check, look for grammar mistakes, and so on. Grammarly is using AI. If they had to add an invisible watermark, everything I produce will be <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/ben-thompson-ai-watermarking-anthropic-claude-2026-8">labeled as AI</a> because I'm using Grammarly.</p><p>I get the intention of the regulation, but I think it's the wrong answer to a real problem.</p><h2 id="b7bcee45-0ef6-4691-a348-35dfdf215174" data-toc-id="b7bcee45-0ef6-4691-a348-35dfdf215174">I built the project in a few hours, but it's turned into a full-time job</h2><p>Text watermarks are based on statistical patterns in word choices. So, big picture, the tool checks for the watermark at the beginning, generates slight variations of the text while preserving meaning, checks again, and reiterates until the watermark is disrupted and no longer flagged. We apply this to images in the same way. Instead of rewriting text, we're rewriting pixels.</p><p>I was able to ship the first version of the project in about five hours and have been working on it pretty much full-time since then. I was able to get the project up quickly because I'd done so much research on the techniques.</p><p>I had also worked with multiple <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/multimodal-generative-ai-pinterest-open-closed-source-llms-2026-4">open-source models</a> in a previous startup, so I had experience assembling various AI tools and piecing the results together. It was for a completely different purpose, but the architecture and the logic were already there for me.</p><p>As the project was gaining traction, a lot of people around the world started to contribute to it. So, I'm starting to get some help, but the first two or three days were relatively intense.</p><h2 id="940d524b-c676-4052-b0a5-d6eb474ef50c" data-toc-id="940d524b-c676-4052-b0a5-d6eb474ef50c">I was not ready to go viral</h2><p>I'm kind of careful with my privacy. I didn't have an active Facebook or <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/instagram-crackdown-meta-ai-glasses-pickup-rizz-videos-moderation-challenges-2026-8">Instagram account</a> before this because that was not my thing. I was really not ready to see influencers talking about my project.</p><p>People are promoting it as if it's perfect. It's not, and it's not a one-shot project. It's going to take months. We'll need to make adjustments when Anthropic releases detectors. A lot of work is in front of us.</p><p>I'm receiving a lot of messages and comments, and 99.9% are very positive. Then there's 0.1% of the comments that are like, "No, but I want to know when something is AI-generated, and you're a bad person."</p><p>There are a lot of subtleties in this conversation. People have a hard time getting that I'm not against content attribution; I'm against the technique and the suggested solution. If you go to the repository and look at the project, it's extremely clear that the intent is not for people to impersonate others or steal content. It's for their own content and for educational purposes.</p><p>I have to reiterate that a lot. There are people who may want to gain visibility from the moment by taking contrarian positions or attacking me. I'm just trying to be nice and explain my position as best I can.</p><h2 id="148f5c70-8957-4797-b682-d94668ab3991" data-toc-id="148f5c70-8957-4797-b682-d94668ab3991">I'm thinking about how to turn this into a business</h2><p>I've started thinking about this a lot. Is it even legally possible to make a commercial product from it? I think so, but I'm not sure, to be honest. The tool is relatively technical and difficult to use correctly. So, making it a simpler solution is one thing to tackle.</p><p>But I'm an entrepreneur, so I think it's natural that, at some point, I would turn this into a business. I don't know how, and I don't know when it'll happen, but it probably will. It makes sense.</p><p>This expanded from just a silly open-source project in a corner of the internet to a real topic of conversation. Aside from the tool itself, I think this going viral says something about how people feel about <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/ai-watermarks-claude-debate-reasons-for-against-2026-8">AI watermarking</a>. I think this conversation should've happened before the regulation came into effect, but I'm happy it's happening right now. It's an important one.</p><p><em>Do you have a story to share about how you're responding to AI watermarks? If so, please reach out to the reporter at</em> <a target="_blank" href="mailto:aapplegate@businessinsider.com"><em><u>aapplegate@businessinsider.com</u></em></a><em>.</em></p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/created-viral-ai-watermark-remover-after-anthropics-announcement-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>When my brother had kids, I didn't even want to meet them. It made me realize why I don't want children of my own.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-23T11:17:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/never-wanted-kids-brother-had-twins-question-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a8771818a99fa493d60e905?format=jpeg" height="1832" width="2443" alt="Jamie valentino on a boat with water behind him"><figcaption>The author doesn&#39;t want children.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Jamie Valentino</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>I never wanted kids; instead, I preferred to live my life by myself.</li><li>But then my brother had twins, and it made me question why I stay away from kids.</li><li>I realized they represent how I'm getting older, but I made room in my life for my nephews anyway.</li></ul><p>I've been saying I <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/dont-want-kids-my-partner-did-we-broke-up-2026-8">don't want kids</a> since I was a kid myself. In fact, as I got older, I became convinced I didn't even like being around them.</p><p>It wasn't something I ever had to think twice about in my 20s, but since entering my 30s, it feels impossible to avoid, especially with taunts of <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/marriage-parenthood-hack-tip-weekly-office-hours-2025-1">marriage and parenthood</a> through my friends and family.</p><p>The biggest window into that life has been my baby brother having babies of his own. Seeing him build the life of his dreams made me question whether I'd be enough as a household of one.</p><h2 id="96c47779-8a87-444e-953e-1926ca657965" data-toc-id="96c47779-8a87-444e-953e-1926ca657965">I thought not wanting kids was just a personal preference</h2><p>I don't hate kids in the same way I don't <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/dont-like-dogs-messed-up-dating-life-2024-6">hate dogs</a>, but I've never had a desire to clean up after either one.</p><p>Sure, you might judge me for comparing <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/enjoying-parenting-raising-tweens-teens-2026-8">raising a kid</a> to caring for a dog, but that's my point. If I couldn't commit to the responsibilities of a pet, what kind of father would I be?</p><p>And that's exactly why I'm keeping my genes to myself, so my life remains mine through whatever older people have, unsolicited, assured me are my best years.</p><p>Although being a guy has spared me from my friends and family openly treating me like a spinster, I've noticed how quickly my self-focused life seems to lose meaning in the eyes of people choosing to dedicate their <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/change-mid-career-how-know-time-pivot-30s-40s-50s-2026-12">30s and 40s</a> to their next of kin.</p><h2 id="7ce0507c-42a5-4e8f-87e6-9bc05894352b" data-toc-id="7ce0507c-42a5-4e8f-87e6-9bc05894352b">My brother was expecting twins</h2><p>Having a lot of siblings with a young mother made me feel confident I had enough people who were bound by blood to me.</p><p>But then my brother announced that he and his wife were <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/terrified-having-twins-postpartum-depression-how-focusing-myself-changed-everything-2026-3">expecting twins</a>. I was excited for them.</p><p>However, I didn't realize how drained I had become by the expectation that my travel plans should revolve around other people's happily-ever-afters. Most recently, that meant RSVPing no to a <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/skipped-destination-wedding-no-plus-one-single-guest-2025-4">friend's wedding</a> in Colombia after she expected me to travel without a plus-one. I went to Hawaii on a friendmoon instead.</p><p>Now I found myself skipping my little brother's coed baby shower to attend New York Fashion Week. They had planned it a month before, and I didn't feel the need to cancel a trip I'd planned six months earlier.</p><p>It was just my latest act of rebellion against being absorbed as a minor character inside someone else's white picket fence.</p><h2 id="48265f9d-87ef-46c1-8ba9-39c0631c495a" data-toc-id="48265f9d-87ef-46c1-8ba9-39c0631c495a">I first didn't even want to meet my nephews</h2><p>I didn't realize how much deeper my discomfort around children went until I avoided visiting my newborn nephews. Rather than feeling connected to them, I found myself repelled by the idea that our <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/family-planning-kids-difficult-self-employed-freelancer-2026-4">family plans</a> would revolve around the household with children.</p><p>It was a selfish thought, I know. But in the past, my little brother had called most of my joys, including fashion, nightlife, and the pursuit of greatness in my career, empty.</p><p>He was one of the kindest people I knew, and he wasn't criticizing my ambitions so much as the superficiality that often accompanied them.</p><p>Vanity was, after all, one of my flaws, which is what made children my kryptonite. They represented the next generation, the next in line to find purpose and meaning in this world. Looking at them reminded me that my own turn would be over eventually.</p><h2 id="38a5e58e-fd98-4814-ae03-9ab62a39bf06" data-toc-id="38a5e58e-fd98-4814-ae03-9ab62a39bf06">I finally paid my nephews a visit</h2><p>In a way, watching a child grow up is the most tangible way a person can be faced with their own mortality.</p><p>"Everyone around us is a mirror reflecting a piece of ourselves, and it sounds like children mirror your fear of running out of time to do all the things you want to do in life," my career-driven friend Manika texted me. She understood me deeply because she had recently frozen her eggs.</p><p>When I finally allowed myself to meet my nephews, I couldn't believe how much more whole I felt in their presence. I wasn't empty before, but I felt fuller.</p><p>These babies and their mother were a perfect addition to <em>my</em> family.</p><p>If anything, I realized there had never been any pressure to live my life a certain way beyond the expectations I had projected onto it myself.</p><p>Life is not necessarily long, but it is wide, and there is room for a lot of wonderful things, even on your own, if you open your heart, confront your insecurities, and embrace every version of happiness without sacrificing your own.</p><p>I didn't need to want kids to make room for them in my life.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/never-wanted-kids-brother-had-twins-question-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>
    <published>2026-08-23T11:17:01Z</published>

    <title>I was burning out as a founder. My summer interns changed everything about the way I work.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-23T11:15:58Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/burnout-startup-founder-interns-changed-everything-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a885a3f8a99fa493d60ec2a?format=jpeg" height="1086" width="1448" alt="Bryan Reed with his interns"><figcaption>Bryan Reed (right) created a close bond with his marketing interns this summer.<p class="copyright">Bryan Reed</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Bryan Reed is a Gen Z startup founder who hired three Gen Z summer interns to help with marketing.</li><li>They worked long hours and figured out ways to boost their productivity and support one another.</li><li>Reed says their close bond made him happier, and he's since changed his approach to work.</li></ul><p><em>This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Bryan Reed, a 24-year-old startup founder based in New York City. It's been edited for length and clarity.</em></p><p>I was <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/investment-banking-professional-burned-out-pivoted-to-portfolio-career-cure-2026-8">burning out</a> this spring. </p><p>In July of 2025, my cofounder and I created Freeport Markets, a trading app that lets people trade international stocks 24/7. </p><p>As a cofounder, I spent my days grinding, eating, staying up late, and doing it all again the next day. I was unhappy with my routine and working mostly alone, because my cofounder and I handle separate tasks and I only work with our engineer occasionally.</p><p>This summer flipped everything, when we brought in three <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/summer-interns-ai-career-ladder-2026-8">college-aged summer interns</a> to work on marketing.</p><p>What started out as dinners together turned into gym trips, movie nights, and late-night reading sessions. They made me excited to go to work again, and our bond made us better problem solvers and more productive.</p><p>Now that the interns are gone, I've changed how I approach work.</p><h2 id="0138615f-d7fe-47e7-a78a-2d40a46228bc" data-toc-id="0138615f-d7fe-47e7-a78a-2d40a46228bc">Being a founder can feel isolating</h2><p>The internship was a very non-traditional arrangement. To be more cost-effective, we had the interns live together in an <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/rent-stabilized-apartment-new-york-city-cant-leave-benefits-drawbacks-2026-8">apartment in NYC</a> and work from our uptown office. The internship was paid hourly, and we also covered their food and housing.</p><p>While I expected to see them for occasional weekend events and for meals, I didn't anticipate hanging out as frequently for evening workouts, movies, and reading, but we hit it off so well. We'd sometimes spend the whole day together from about 10 a.m. to 11 p.m.</p><p>In a small startup, everyone is thinking about the same things 24/7, so it feels natural to spend time with people in the same headspace. Other people probably wouldn't understand; however, if a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/tiny-ai-startup-hired-private-chef-costs-productivity-2026-5">small startup</a> like this isn't spending 12 hours a day together, I wouldn't expect it to be successful.</p><h2 id="0d5ca585-afaa-40f6-92be-53d6171b9506" data-toc-id="0d5ca585-afaa-40f6-92be-53d6171b9506">Our bond helped us work better together</h2><p>I remember reading something a while ago that one of the determining factors in how long you'll keep your mental performance as you age, and even in your lifespan, is <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/longevity-antiaging-friendship-social-interaction-relationships-2023-9">how social you are</a>. I became happier to spend more time in the office because I was looking forward to waking up and seeing everyone. It had a huge impact on my mental wellness and performance.</p><p>As friendships grew, we'd hit the gym together or watch movies. We started talking more about personal life things, growing closer throughout the summer.</p><p>Connecting more on a personal level translated to more success when working. I think it helped them disagree and push back on me and each other without it feeling weird, which ultimately led us to better results.</p><h2 id="21bec546-411a-4650-8910-50844c71fe7d" data-toc-id="21bec546-411a-4650-8910-50844c71fe7d">Using phones less and reading more helped us boost productivity</h2><p>At one point, to help us scroll our phones less, I decided to implement 90-minute reading sessions three times a week after dinner. We basically traded the time we'd normally use to watch a movie or get more work done to do some reading-for-pleasure together as a group. I read with them, usually fantasy and sci-fi, because I thought it would be silly to expect them to do it and not do it myself.</p><p>We'd also put our phones away when we were eating together, which helped us stay present. That presence opened up the doors for us to talk more about big ideas and gave us space to come up with more creative approaches, like our marketing ads near all the big finance firms in the Financial District.</p><h2 id="b26a7a80-916d-4d08-85d5-dde8d324add8" data-toc-id="b26a7a80-916d-4d08-85d5-dde8d324add8">Now that the interns are gone, I've adapted my lifestyle</h2><p>It's so hard to know how exactly I'll approach my next group of interns because I think this last group was very special. I'll continue to build a group dynamic and encourage activities like working out or having meals together because I think it's important for them to have structure and to build bonds.</p><p>Now that the interns are gone, I'm back to working mostly alone and with my small team. I'm trying to fill up my schedule with more evening plans, like dinners or events. I also started hosting poker tournaments on weekends, which have been super fun and great for meeting new customers.</p><p>I've realized that being social makes me happier <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/tips-work-life-balance-work-psychologists-2024-8">without detracting from productivity</a>. I'm happier, and that makes me want to keep pushing with my startup.</p><p><em>Do you have a story to share about how your interns changed your approached to work? If so, please reach out to the editor mlogan@businessinsider.com.</em></p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/burnout-startup-founder-interns-changed-everything-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>Gen Z, stop Venmoing your friends over half-eaten avocados and follow these 2 rules instead</title>
    <updated>2026-08-23T10:41:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/rule-for-gen-z-venmo-bill-splitting-etiquette-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a7e3245c78818eff7d2cce6?format=jpeg" height="4000" width="6000" alt="Hands reach for seasoned fries beside a burger and ketchup in a cardboard takeout box on a wooden table."><figcaption><p class="copyright">mihailomilovanovic/Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li><em>This post originally appeared in the BI Today newsletter.</em></li><li><em>You can sign up for </em><a target="_blank" rel="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/subscription/newsletter/insider-today" data-autoaffiliated="false"><em>Business Insider's daily newsletter here</em></a><em>.</em></li></ul><h2 id="11850be2-84e0-4d2d-bc14-a7b71271d9fa" data-toc-id="11850be2-84e0-4d2d-bc14-a7b71271d9fa"><strong>Splitting the difference</strong></h2><p><strong>Most people settle their taxes in April. I used to do a bit of accounting every Sunday morning.</strong></p><p>My weekly routine wasn't with the IRS. Instead, I'd settle up with a hodgepodge of friends I crossed paths with over the weekend. From Uber rides to rounds of drinks to late-night takeout, there was always some combination of debits and credits that needed sorting out through bleary eyes and a throbbing headache.</p><p>It's been a while since I played that game. (Two kids, a move to the suburbs, and being on the wrong side of 30 will do that to you.) But I still thoroughly enjoyed my newsletter colleague <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/author/amanda-yen?follow-me">Amanda Yen's</a> piece about <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/gen-z-friendship-venmo-etiquette-splitting-bills-money-manners-2026-8">Gen Z nickel-and-diming their friends</a> with Venmo requests.</p><p>In a lot of ways, I relate to Gen Z's plight. Early in your career, and especially in this economy, everything feels impossibly expensive. Paying for anything you didn't specifically agree to can feel like a raw deal.</p><p>But everyone has their limits, and for me, that limit is charging a friend 25 cents for eating half an avocado. (Like I said, <a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/gen-z-friendship-venmo-etiquette-splitting-bills-money-manners-2026-8">you have to read Amanda's story</a>.)</p><p>So, Gen Z Venmo veterans, I have some advice.</p><p>First, adopt this phrase: <em>It all comes out in the wash.</em></p><p>Yes, there will be times when you get the short end of the stick. When everyone's ordering vodka seltzers and you're just ordering seltzers. It happens.</p><p>But at some point, the tables will turn. Someone will spot your cover charge at the bar. (Is that even still a thing? Damn, I'm old.) Or buy you a few slices of pizza.</p><p>And when you try to pay them back, you'll hear this glorious phrase: "Let's just call it even."</p><p>"But Dan," you say, "I'm ALWAYS getting shafted by these friends."</p><p>In that case, I offer my second piece of advice: <em>Normalize no.</em></p><p>Because if the people you consistently find yourself going out with are the ones taking advantage of you, those aren't people you should be going out with in the first place. Maybe you just recalibrate how you hang out with them. Maybe you cut them out entirely.</p><p>Whatever the case, I'm confident these two rules will leave you with a friend group that doesn't wreck your finances. And with any luck, as your career progresses and you get some raises, you'll eventually start having a different argument with friends:</p><p>Who <em>gets</em> to pay the bill?</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/rule-for-gen-z-venmo-bill-splitting-etiquette-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>Steve Hanke has 'no problem' with his students using AI to cheat — as he's an 'old fox' who easily sniffs them out</title>
    <updated>2026-08-23T10:24:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/steve-hanke-ai-students-chatgpt-cheating-homework-university-education-chatbots-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a886d768a99fa493d60ed02?format=jpeg" height="2056" width="2741" alt="Steve Hanke"><figcaption>Steve Hanke says he&#39;s an &quot;old fox&quot; when it comes to detecting AI use.<p class="copyright">Steve Hanke</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>AI tools like ChatGPT have made it more tempting than ever for students to cheat on assignments.</li><li>Steve Hanke, a veteran Johns Hopkins professor, says he's an "old fox" who can sniff out AI use.</li><li>Hanke said it's a red flag when a student's work doesn't match their writing skills or knowledge.</li></ul><p>It's simpler than ever for students to <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/ai-chatgpt-homework-cheating-machine-sam-altman-openai-2024-8">cheat on their homework</a> using ChatGPT or another AI chatbot. But one professor says he has no trouble sniffing out machine-written work.</p><p>"I have absolutely no problem with AI and students," <a target="" class="" href="https://markets.businessinsider.com/news/stocks/wall-street-jobs-hanke-johns-hopkins-class-buffett-investing-valuation-2023-11">Steve Hanke</a>, who's been teaching at Johns Hopkins University for nearly 60 years, told Business Insider.</p><p>Hanke described himself as an "old fox" who finds it "very easy" to differentiate between a student's work and a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/chatgpt-for-teens-test-help-cheat-homework-2026-8">chatbot's output</a>.</p><p>The professor of applied economics, who served on President Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers, pointed to the "poor writing skills" of today's students, even at elite universities, as the main reason he doesn't struggle.</p><p>Hanke said it's "blatant when a student submission has been generated by AI."</p><p>He also has a fairly good sense of his students' knowledge of economics, making it "pretty easy to spot" when a piece of work doesn't match their skill level, he said.</p><p>"The only problem that AI poses is that it requires the old fox to be on guard, more than would have been the case sans AI," he said.</p><p>Drusilla Blackman, a former dean of admissions at Harvard and Columbia, echoed Hanke's view during a <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/drusilla-blackman-admissions-advice-wealth-parenting-children-college-strategy-careers-2026-8">recent interview</a> with Business Insider.</p><p>Blackman said that it's almost always "evident" to an educator when a student has used AI, as what they've submitted doesn't match their standard of work, writing, or critical thinking.</p><p>"If they write something that is not proportional to that, it is detectible," said the founder of Deans of Admissions, a group that advises families on how to get their children into top-flight universities in the US and Britain.</p><p>Beyond detecting chatbot-generated work, several teachers <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/teachers-change-curriculum-assignments-student-ai-cheating-2025-6">told Business Insider last year</a> that they were using AI defensively to develop AI-resistant assignments, and even reverting to handwritten assignments to discourage use of the tools.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/steve-hanke-ai-students-chatgpt-cheating-homework-university-education-chatbots-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>I keep accidentally DMing TikToks to people. One of these days, it's going to ruin my life.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-23T10:05:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/tiktok-accidental-sending-dm-issue-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a7655aa8fcc2e955f7dea5d?format=jpeg" height="1414" width="2121" alt="woman in sweater upset at hpone"><figcaption>Of all the ways I embarrass myself with my phone, sending accidental DMs on TikTok is one of the worst.<p class="copyright">Juan Algar/Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>I somehow keep DMing TikToks to the same person by accident.</li><li>It's really embarrassing. Aaaaagghhhhh!</li><li>I'm not totally sure how it happens, but it seems to be from long-pressing the screen.</li></ul><p>This spring, I saw a TikTok that intrigued me. Befuddled me, maybe I should say. <a target="_blank" class="" href="https://www.tiktok.com/@alishamarie/video/7627555756795104525?is_from_webapp=1&amp;sender_device=pc&amp;web_id=7481283243075421727">A woman sat on her bed</a> and screamed into a pillow. The text across the middle of the screen read, "this feels worse than texting your ex." A pinned comment said "She def doesn't know about this audio lol."</p><p>Confusing, right? I know my description doesn't make any sense. Neither did the video. That was the problem.</p><p>I tried to tap into the caption at the bottom to see what comment the video was in response to, so I could understand the context (turns out it was about an earlier video she made about her Coachella outfit, where she accidentally used a thematically inappropriate song playing over it, kind of a let-down, to be honest).</p><p>But instead, somehow I tapped something that immediately sent the video as a DM to one of my contacts, Maura Johnston.</p><p>This was kind of embarrassing, but it also wasn't the first time I've accidentally sent TikToks to Johnson. In fact, I've accidentally sent her so many TikToks that this wasn't even among the more embarrassing ones I've done. I've also accidentally sent her ones about lesbian dating, birth control pills, storytimes about college hookups, and the sound an MRI machine makes.</p><p>Johnston isn't a close friend that I DM with often. She's more of a friendly professional acquaintance — a fellow journalist — but she isn't someone I'd normally send videos about the pros and cons of hormonal birth control to. In fact, I wouldn't normally send most of those videos to my closest friends — they weren't particularly funny or relevant to my friends or me.</p><p>That's part of what was so embarrassing about these accidentally DM'd TikToks — they were the kind of feed-filler stuff that normally isn't send-worthy.</p><p>One comfort in all of this is that I know I'm not alone. My colleague, Peter Kafka, also keeps accidentally sending me TikToks. The thing is, the videos he sends are pretty normal — mostly news or sports clips. This just makes me feel even worse about how comparatively embarrassing my accidentally sent videos are.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a7653040c6c5a263f3a7d40?format=jpeg" height="741" width="1263" alt="long press tiktok screenshot"><figcaption>If you tap and hold the arrow, it opens up the avatar to several of your recent friends.<p class="copyright">TikTok</p></figcaption></figure><p>I've asked TikTok if they were aware of this problem or why it's happening. I wish I could give you clear advice about how to stop doing this, I'm not 100% sure how I'm doing it in the first place. There seem to be two separate ways a person might accidentally send a DM.</p><p>The first is long-pressing the arrow button on the side of a video. When you merely tap it, it opens a menu to copy the link. But if you press and hold, it opens an instant DM option with the avatars of three of your friends. From there, you can send it as a DM without having to write a message or any extra taps.</p><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a7653b00c0bf4e8be522ffe?format=jpeg" height="1579" width="1287" alt="how i send vdieos in tiktok"><figcaption>When you long-press the bottom of a video, it opens this other menu with easy-to-DM options.<p class="copyright">TikTok</p></figcaption></figure><p>The second option is more likely for videos with long captions, where you mean to tap "more" to expand the full caption.</p><p>When you long-press the bottom of the screen on a video, it opens a menu. When I do this on a video in my normal FYP, there's no option to send the video — but if I do it from a video inside a hashtag search, the menu looks different — and has a list of those people to easily send it to.</p><p>Although I'm not 100% sure, my guess is that I'm doing these accidental DMs when I tap the "more" button too long, opening this menu.</p><p>Thankfully, Johnston has been very kind about this. I had immediately apologized to her for all the errant videos, and she totally understood — she's done it, too.</p><p>If there's any upside to this embarrassing situation, it's that it's given me a reason to chat with her. There are certainly people out there whom I would be much more embarrassed to accidentally send TikToks to!</p><p>In some ways, I feel that this is my penance for wasting time on TikTok. Rolling the dice on occasionally getting shamed is a good way for me to manage my screen time!</p><p>Be careful out there, folks.</p><div class="read-original">Read the original article on <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/tiktok-accidental-sending-dm-issue-2026-8">Business Insider</a></div></content>

    <title>I'm an executive coach. I tell clients not to spend Sunday night preparing for work.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-23T09:55:01Z</updated>
    <id>https://www.businessinsider.com/executive-coach-sunday-night-work-monday-morning-routine-2026-8</id>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/6a88776b8a99fa493d60edb2?format=jpeg" height="3024" width="4032" alt="Shane Arthur"><figcaption>On Fridays, executive coach Shane Arthur tries to walk in the woods to review his week and prepare for the next.<p class="copyright">Courtesy of Shane Arthur</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Executive coach Shane Arthur advises clients not to spend Sunday nights prepping for the week.</li><li>He blocks Monday <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/founder-two-days-week-without-meetings-boosts-productivity-2024-9" data-autoaffiliated="false">morning meetings</a> to ease into the workweek and Friday afternoons to wind down.</li><li>Arthur said that while there are rules, employees have a bit more freedom than they sometimes take.</li></ul><p><em>Shane Arthur, an </em><a target="_blank" href="https://www.arthurcoaching.com/"><em>executive coach</em></a><em> in Raleigh, North Carolina, advises clients to avoid working on Sundays — and to start their workweeks by avoiding</em><strong><em> </em></strong><em>meetings on Monday mornings. The following has been edited for brevity and clarity.</em></p><p>I believe in startup and shutdown routines for your week. On Monday mornings, I get my coffee, my journal, and my laptop. I take it slow and build my way into my week. It takes two to three hours.</p><p>Working on Sundays is something I've seen people talking about on LinkedIn, as in, "This is how to make your week work." The idea is that if you crush the prep on Sunday night, the week goes so well.</p><p>Don't do that. Many of my clients are business owners, CEOs, and executives who are consistently working too much.</p><p>I own my business, so I have the freedom to book the hours I want. I find that when I wake up on a Monday morning, get the kids fed, and my wife or I drop them off at school, I need to recharge a little bit. To jump into client calls at 9 o'clock in the morning is tough.</p><p>I'll do that on other days of the week, but Monday mornings are a protected space for me. I coach my clients to do the same thing if they have the freedom to do so. I tell my clients to help their teams think about this, too, so that it can trickle down a bit.</p><p>Even if you're not the boss, I think employees have a bit more freedom than they sometimes take. I understand that there are rules you have to follow, but at least the <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/cutting-work-meetings-can-make-you-happier-and-more-productive-2024-7">first hour of every Monday</a> and the last hour of every Friday is key.</p><p>The trick is <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/workers-spending-less-time-in-meetings-productivity-2024-4">not having meetings</a>. As long as nobody is demanding your time in that window, you get to choose how you use it. That is where the magic is.</p><h2 id="31ae9dae-f384-443f-9476-414e99b5cdf6" data-toc-id="31ae9dae-f384-443f-9476-414e99b5cdf6"><strong>I used to try to do everything between calls</strong></h2><p>On Fridays, I try not to take late afternoon calls. If the weather's nice, I'll walk in the woods. I'm looking back at my week, going through each day and remembering: <em>Are there any to-dos? I'm looking ahead to next week. Are there any things that need to be prepped for? Anything to confirm?</em> I think of it as general housekeeping.</p><p>I have to not fill the day because if I'm on a call as I'm walking in the house at 5 o'clock on Friday, I'm pretty distracted for that first hour. It's still on my mind. My energy is still in that place.</p><p>I used to try to do everything in the two minutes between calls. I don't anymore. I wait until the end of the day or the end of the week to catch up on all that stuff.</p><p>When I'm coaching, I tell people to identify the most important things for the day and do those first. Some clients get so into calls and being available that they finish the day, and the important things aren't done. Then they go home and <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/tech-worker-shares-why-she-took-career-break-2026-3">do them at night</a>. I'm not interested in working like that or helping other people work like that.</p><p>If you're working a 40- or 45-hour week, if you can just hold on to the first hour and last hour, your whole experience is different. I think you will end up being more productive, but that's not my goal. My goal is to make it all flow more smoothly. A well-organized, <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/wednesday-most-popular-day-work-meetings-avoid-overload-2023-12">structured 35-hour workweek</a> beats a rushed, 45-hour workweek every time.</p><h2 id="fd61bfa4-7261-4572-b564-1aff3bcdc51c" data-toc-id="fd61bfa4-7261-4572-b564-1aff3bcdc51c"><strong>We're always holding work and family in tension</strong></h2><p>There was a CEO I coached for a couple of years. I ran into him at a golf tournament and met his wife. She gave me a bear hug and started talking about how much their family life had changed because of how he was showing up.</p><p>Most of my clients are always thinking about all the people they're taking care of, the <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/one-on-one-weekly-meeting-with-boss-mistakes-2024-1">people they're responsible for</a>. We're always holding work and family in tension. I'm not asking people to choose family 100% of the time.</p><p>The way we work has changed. It's much easier to always be connected. We <a target="" class="" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/what-rto-personality-type-are-you-2026-8">used to have offices</a> and set work hours, and for many people, that's no longer true. That connectivity has led people to reach out in ways that would have been inappropriate 30 years ago.     <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/61d6ece837afc20019ac72f1?format=jpeg" height="2001" width="3000" alt="A man walks in front of a Blockbuster video store."><figcaption>A Blockbuster movie video rental store 2013.<p class="copyright">Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images</p></figcaption></figure><ul class="summary-list"><li>Falling foot traffic and rising online competition have led thousands of stores to close.</li><li>Once household names like Blockbuster, Bed Bath &amp; Beyond, and Eddie Bauer are now retail history.</li><li>BI rounded up dozens of once-beloved brands that no longer have a significant brick-and-mortar presence.</li></ul><p>Retail is a tough business.</p><p>One day, your favorite brand can be riding high and enjoying strong sales from loyal customers, while the next it's fighting for survival and fending off creditors.</p><p>Emerging trends, changing shopping patterns, and new e-commerce players are increasingly reshuffling the game.</p><p>Here's a look back at some of the retail brands whose stores once greeted thousands of people each day.</p><p>Some are now consigned to retail's history books, while others still exist online. Either way, they're a tiny fraction of what they once were.</p><p><strong><em>What stores do you miss most? Tell us in the comments below:</em></strong></p><div id="slideshow"><div class="slide"><div class="slide-title">Blockbuster</div><div class="slide-image"><figure><img src="https://i.insider.com/5b89b85c5c5e52fe368b531f?format=jpeg" height="1485" width="1981" charset="" alt="Blockbuster"><figcaption><p class="copyright">Getty</p></figcaption></figure></div><div class="slide-content"><p><a target="_blank" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/rise-and-fall-of-blockbuster">Blockbuster started in 1985</a> and acquired the Sound Warehouse and Music Plus music chains to create Blockbuster Music in 1992.
